GRASP: A Greenwashing Recognition and Scoring Pipeline for Structured BRSR Disclosures in India  Yugchhaya Galphat, Purab Keshwani, Khushi Dayaramani, Ronit Chugwani, and Karan Sarani  Computer Department, Vivekanand Education Society’s Institute of Technology Mumbai, India  yugchhaya.dhote@ves.ac.in; 2023.purab.keshwani@ves.ac.in 2023.khushi.dayaramani@ves.ac.in; 2023.ronit.chugwani@ves.ac.in 2023.karan.sarani@ves.ac.in  Abstract  The Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report (BRSR) brings sustainability infor- mation into a common format for India’s listed companies. Reviewing these reports requires analysts to connect written claims with filed figures, reporting periods, and industry context. GRASP organises this task through a seven-part pipeline. Structured digital filings (XBRL) are collected and stored with company and period details. Filing tags and concept mappings provide training labels. A BERT model adapted to BRSR text classifies passages under nine principles. Word lists and sentence similarity identify vague statements, while numerical and assurance checks produce linked review records. Principle mapping summarises the model’s support for each reporting principle. A four-part Transparency Score supports company and sector comparisons, and an application programming interface provides access to the outputs. The saved results cover 1,164 companies. On 6,201 test passages from companies excluded from supervised training, the classifier agrees with filing-derived labels in 93.00% of cases. The Trans- parency Score correlates with 20 historical human ratings at   r   = 0 . 6314. Linked passages, score breakdowns, and peer comparisons help analysts follow the evidence and prioritise disclosures for review.  Keywords:   BRSR; sustainability disclosure; weak supervision; BERT; vagueness detection; transparency scoring; sector benchmarking.  1   Introduction  India’s Business Responsibility and Sustainability Reporting framework gives environmental, social, and governance disclosures a common structure. A 2021 circular from the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) made BRSR reporting mandatory for the top 1,000 listed companies by market capitalisation from financial year 2022–23. The framework covers nine principles of responsible business conduct. Essential indicators are mandatory, while leadership indicators are voluntary [1]. A common format helps organise reports, but cannot establish whether every response is complete or correct. A data analyst must complete several manual steps when reviewing a filing. First, a passage must be found and assigned to a topic. Next, a relevant numerical value must be located and checked against the reporting year, unit, and group covered. Comparing companies adds another challenge 1

because business activities and applicable reporting items differ.   Repeating these steps across hundreds of filings takes substantial time. For example, a statement that   water use decreased   needs a matching water measure, business boundary, and comparison period before the claim can be assessed. Automated text analysis can reduce this workload. ClimateBERT identifies climate-related language and selected disclosure categories. ChatReport retrieves report passages and answers reporting questions with source links. ESGReveal extracts structured information from narrative reports [2, 3, 4].   These methods help organise large report collections.   Three questions remain when building a connected workflow for Indian structured filings. The first question is   how to connect a claim with evidence . A phrase detector can find a promise, and a text-similarity model can identify an environmental topic. A supporting figure must also match the claim’s meaning, period, and reporting context. The second question is   how to organise training labels . Filing tags and concept maps provide a repeatable assignment procedure, with the label source recorded for each passage. The third question is   how to interpret a company score . The calculation, included items, sector group, and reference source provide this context. GRASP brings these requirements together in a connected BRSR workflow with clearly defined tests [5, 6]. GRASP addresses the first question by storing narrative passages and structured facts under the same filing. Language checks flag passages for review, while numerical and assurance checks keep the linked sentence and reported item available for inspection. The second question is addressed by recording three label sources and comparing results by source, company, and excluded question concept. The third question is addressed by showing four score components and comparisons within recorded sectors. The contribution combines links to filed evidence, filing-derived training labels, detailed evaluation, and a score with a visible breakdown. The study provides a 42,409-sample dataset with documented weak labels and separate companies for supervised training, validation, and testing. The classifier is assessed by label source and on concepts excluded from training. The language detector is evaluated with fixed settings, while the numerical checks supply linked review records. Company-score results move from one worked example to the full financial-sector group and all recorded sectors. The evaluation identifies the data group and reference source for each model result, human-score comparison, and service check. The remaining sections of this paper follow the workflow from earlier research to practical use. Section 2 reviews related methods and Indian disclosure studies. Section 3 presents the proposed solution and the flow from filing data to review outputs. Section 4 explains the seven modules and score calculations. Section 5 defines the test data and reports the audited model results. Section 6 presents the four reporting levels, from one company to all sector groups. Section 7 discusses output interpretation and practical use. Section 8 summarises the findings and future work.  2   Literature Review  Automated sustainability analysis includes several tasks: finding relevant passages, identifying commitments, checking whether a statement is specific, retrieving evidence, and organising results. These tasks provide useful signals, but a language signal alone does not prove that a company has misled a reader. Calamai et al. review these tasks and identify continuing problems with available datasets and evaluation methods [5]. The review below keeps each task separate from a claim of verified greenwashing.  2.1   Language models and training labels  BERT learns word meaning from the surrounding text and can then be trained for a labelled classification task [7]. Gururangan et al. show that further training on domain and task text can 2

improve several classification tasks [8]. This finding supports adapting a model to sustainability reports. Lower language-model loss, however, does not alone establish better principle classification. Sentence-BERT represents each sentence as a numerical vector, allowing sentence meanings to be compared with cosine similarity [9]. Similarity helps find related language, but does not confirm that a statement is supported by evidence. Weak supervision uses rules to reduce manual labelling.   Snorkel combines labelling rules and estimates uncertainty in the resulting labels [10]. GRASP uses a simpler fixed assignment from filing tags and concept names. An incorrect assignment can therefore repeat across many examples. Kapoor and Narayanan explain how data leakage and weak evaluation design can make machine- learning results appear stronger than the evidence supports [11]. This motivates checks on company overlap, repeated text, label sources, and saved-model loading.  2.2   Climate topics, commitments, and communication quality  ClimaText provides labelled sentences for climate-topic detection [12]. A topic label helps select relevant text, but does not assess the support for a claim.   ClimateBERT adds pretraining on climate text and evaluates climate-language tasks [2]. Bingler et al. use ClimateBERT to study selective and unclear reporting under the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD) framework [13]. A later study relates climate-related cheap talk, meaning statements with limited substance, to climate initiatives, emissions growth, and reputation risk [14]. These studies already connect corporate language with performance-related information. The contribution of GRASP should therefore be stated for the specific BRSR workflow. ClimateBERT-NetZero uses approximately 3,500 expert-labelled examples, target classification, and question answering to study net-zero and reduction commitments [15]. Finding a target and extracting the target details are separate tasks. Vinella et al. use generated labels and a fine-tuned ClimateBERT model to study greenwashing risk [16].   Generated labels increase the available training data, but the evaluation still depends on how those labels were produced.   The same concern applies to AI-assisted concept mapping in GRASP.  2.3   Report-level tools and Indian disclosure studies  ChatReport combines language-model assistance, report passages, and expert feedback to support disclosure review [3]. ESGReveal uses document preparation, standard questions, and language- model agents to extract structured information from ESG reports [4]. Both studies support the value of a connected review tool. GRASP starts from structured XBRL facts, where values already have filing identifiers and numerical context. For these available fields, page-layout extraction is not required. Shankar and Xu describe a BERT sentence classifier trained with expert labels for Indian sustain- ability reports [17]. The source is an SSRN working paper posted in 2025, with a manuscript dated 2024. Garg et al. review BRSR disclosures from 1,012 Indian businesses for 2022–23 [6]. This institutional report provides Indian reporting context and a broad review of disclosure practices. The report is not a machine-learning detection benchmark.  2.4   Design choices for the BRSR workflow  The literature supports three choices: connect evidence to filing identifiers, record how training labels are obtained, and show how a company score is calculated. GRASP combines these choices through a filing database, a nine-principle classifier, review flags, and sector comparisons. The evaluation compares label sources, principle categories, and company groups. Table 1 summarises 3

Narrative passages and numerical facts are stored together with company and reporting details.   An analyst can therefore move from a flagged statement or a score component to the underlying disclosure. The central idea is to connect language analysis with reported evidence and present the resulting records in one review workflow. The design responds to the three questions introduced in Section 1.   Evidence links connect a passage with reported values. Recorded label sources explain how training examples receive principle assignments. A visible score breakdown and sector comparison explain a company’s position. The contribution brings these functions together for Indian BRSR filings, with a defined role for each model, rule, and calculation. The seven modules shown in Figure 1 follow this design. Filing acquisition and storage create the common data record. Narrative selection removes unusable text and derives weak training labels from principle tags and concept mappings, including the documented AI-assisted assignments. Domain adaptation prepares BERT for BRSR language, and supervised training produces a classifier for the nine reporting principles. The analysis modules use the stored passages and facts for different purposes.   Word lists and sentence similarity identify vague language. Numerical and assurance checks create separate review records containing the relevant claim and reported item. Principle mapping uses the classifier’s probabilities to summarise support for each principle; a zero-shot method provides the evaluation comparator. The Transparency Score combines Completeness, Specificity, Clarity, and mapped SDG breadth, followed by comparisons within recorded sectors. Principle probabilities and numerical review flags remain separate from the four score components. The service layer makes company records, review flags, principle summaries, score breakdowns, and peer comparisons accessible through an API. Results can be read at four levels: one company, selected companies within a sector, the complete financial-sector group, and all recorded sectors. Available paired filings also support year-by-year comparison.   Section 4 explains the internal working of each module, while Section 5 defines the evidence used to assess the outputs. 5

4.1   Filing acquisition and structured storage  The input consists of BRSR filings in eXtensible Business Reporting Language (XBRL), together with company identifiers.   A download log records completed and failed files so collection can resume after an interruption. The parser reads structured filing data directly. A concept names a reporting item, such as water withdrawal. The context records the company, period, and any reporting categories, while the unit records how a numerical value is measured [18]. This structure keeps a figure linked to the information needed for comparison. The database has three linked record types.   A company record stores the Corporate Identity Number (CIN), name, and industry code. A filing record stores the company link, reporting dates, and source location. A fact record stores the concept, original value, unit, stated precision when available, period, and dimensions. Dimensions are categories such as gender or employment type. A workforce count can therefore retain these categories instead of becoming one combined number. Values are stored as text and converted to numbers only when a calculation requires arithmetic. A company–year uniqueness rule limits duplicate ingestion of the same filing. The output is a searchable database of reported facts. Each value retains a link to the source filing, reported concept, period, and unit. These links support later passage review, numerical comparison, and company-score calculation.  4.2   Narrative selection and weak-label construction  Text candidates come from concepts containing   ExplanatoryTextBlock . Before counting words, the dataset builder removes URLs. At least 15 words of useful content must remain. Bare links, short fragments, and listed non-answers are removed.   These rules define the classifier dataset. The company-scoring modules use different text-length rules, explained in Section 4.6. Classifier passages and scoring passages are therefore different groups of text. Principle labels come from three sources, checked in order. An explicit   PrincipleAxis   tag supplies a Section B label. If that tag is unavailable, a Section C concept-to-principle map supplies the label. A numbered   NotesPrincipleX   concept provides the third source. The extension includes 29 AI-assisted assignments, with existing configured mappings taking priority when maps overlap. The process produces taxonomy-derived weak labels rather than independent passage-level expert judgements; the AI-assisted assignments have no completed independent expert verification. Candidates are grouped by company, concept, and cleaned text. Repeated entries with the same label produce one row.   A group with several labels is removed from the single-label dataset. These groups can include passages covering several principles or generic text reused under different questions. The resulting dataset contains 42,409 samples. The CSV records the label source for analysis, while only the passage text enters the classifier. The labelled dataset is split by CIN. Training contains 29,834 passages from 814 companies, validation contains 6,374 passages from 175 companies, and test contains 6,201 passages from 175 companies. No company appears in more than one split. This company-based partition defines the main supervised evaluation. Exact wording shared across different companies is counted separately in the text-overlap check.  4.3   Domain adaptation and principle classification  The encoder starts from   bert-base-uncased .   Masked language modelling adapts BERT to sustainability text: selected word pieces are hidden, and the model learns to predict the missing text. A nine-output classification layer is then added, and labelled training adjusts the model for the nine principles. For a passage   x , the model returns a probability   p k ( x ) for each principle   k . 7

The largest probability gives the Top-1 prediction. The two largest probabilities give the Top-2 candidate list [7, 8].  Model development and component roles.   The final model follows four steps: base BERT, adaptation to BRSR text, supervised training for nine principles, and recovery of the selected seed-99 checkpoint. A checkpoint is a saved set of model parameters. Adaptation changes the parameters while keeping the BERT structure. Fine-tuning adds the classification output layer and updates the encoder. Recovery corrects saved parameter names and verifies loading without further training. MPNet supplies sentence similarity for vagueness checks and the zero-shot comparison. The final audited evaluation uses the recovered BERT classifier; earlier ClimateBERT and ensemble runs belong to the passage-level experiment history. The classifier accepts at most 512 tokens, meaning word pieces produced by the tokenizer. Dynamic padding adds only the padding needed within a batch. Training processes four passages at a time and combines gradients across four such microbatches before updating the model. An epoch is one pass through the training set. Fine-tuning runs for five epochs with learning rate 2   ×   10 − 5 , weight decay 0.01, 300 warmup steps, and cosine learning-rate decay. The learning rate controls update size, warmup raises the rate gradually, and cosine decay then lowers the rate along a smooth curve. Weight decay limits parameter growth. Cross-entropy loss penalises low probability for the reference label. Class weights use the square root of inverse training frequency. Less common classes receive more weight, but the square root limits the increase. A random seed makes the training choices repeatable. Five seeds, 42, 1, 7, 99, and 2024, were compared using validation macro-F1. Seed 99 and checkpoint 7,460 form the audited final classifier. Checkpoint recovery verifies the parameters used for inference. The selected file contains 50 Layer- Norm parameters with older   gamma / beta   names. Recovery changes these names to   weight / bias , requires every parameter to load, and confirms tensor equality after saving and reloading. The test result uses this recovered model. The earlier masked-language-model builder reads text across the company database, and checkpoint-specific adaptation membership has not been verified. The recorded company-separation assertions therefore apply to labelled fine-tuning.  4.4   Vagueness and filing-consistency checks  The risk module produces two kinds of review output. The language branch combines a hedging word list with sentence-similarity checks. The numerical branch produces claim–figure, assurance- gap, and omission records with links to the relevant filing material. Section 5 reports the evaluation group for each measured component.  4.4.1   Hedging words and evidence markers  A hedging word list identifies promises, conditional commitments, unclear time expressions, and progress claims without a measure. Evidence patterns look for percentages, currency amounts, physical quantities, workforce or incident counts, reporting years, named standards, and selected formal governance systems. The code names this marker   has_kpi . This marker includes numerical indicators, named policies, and standards. Specificity records the presence of these details in a passage. The word-list rule flags a passage containing hedging without an evidence marker. For passages longer than 80 words, hedging density, calculated as matches divided by word count, must also reach 0.005. A separate rule flags bare URLs and listed website redirects. The final pattern set requires digits in currency matches, includes MW/GW units and statutory terms, and handles URL redirects explicitly. 8

4.4.2   Comparing sentence meanings  The similarity check uses the   all-mpnet-base-v2   sentence encoder [9, 19]. Each passage is split into sentences. Sentence vectors are compared with two fixed reference sets: vague statements and specific statements. Cosine similarity measures how close two vectors are. Let   v j   be the largest similarity between sentence   j   and a vague reference, and   q j   the largest similarity to a specific reference. The rule selects the sentence with the largest   q j   −   v j   , treating that sentence as the most specific part of the passage. The decision uses the selected sentence. Without an evidence marker, the similarity rule requires  v j   ≥   0 . 42 and   v j   > q j   ; either the word-list rule or this similarity rule can flag the passage. With an evidence marker, flagging requires   v j   ≥   0 . 58 and   v j   −   q j   ≥   0 . 15. A URL-redirect match takes priority. The decision therefore uses the most specific sentence together with the evidence-marker status. The freeze file records the detector version and thresholds before the audited run. The settings remain fixed during evaluation. Batches 1 and 2 form the 80-example development group.  4.4.3   Claim–figure, assurance, and omission checks  The numerical branch checks selected topics, including emissions, water, waste, and non-renewable energy. A sentence must contain both improvement wording and a phrase linked to the measure. A review record is created when the linked filed value increases despite reduction-style wording. The record keeps the sentence, concept, previous and current values, and assurance information. Matching within a sentence reduces accidental links, such as comparing a Scope 2 reduction claim with a Scope 1 increase. The assurance-gap rule links a domain-specific fact with reported assurance information.   The omission rule identifies a prior-period concept without a matching current-period concept. Analyst review compares measure definitions, total versus per-output quantities, units, periods, and business boundaries using the linked filing context. The current assurance-gap implementation selects a domain-matched fact without fully restricting period, unit, and dimension, and treats a text value of zero as absent. The omission rule excludes selected zero-valued prior entries. These selection rules can affect review flags, so context review inspects the original values and reporting categories. The Completeness calculation separately accepts structured zeros as valid responses. Numerical records are reported as rule-generated review signals; the accuracy results in Section 5 cover the language branch.  4.5   Principle mapping and the zero-shot comparator  The mapping service reuses the recovered classifier. The output layer produces nine raw scores, called logits.   Softmax converts these scores into principle probabilities.   Reuse of the trained classifier is called supervised transfer in the evaluation. For passages filed under principle   k , the service averages   p k ( x ) and keeps the lowest-scoring passage for inspection. The company summary averages the available principle means. This value describes model support for the recorded principle assignment. The zero-shot comparison uses MPNet vectors for the same test passages. Final values come from the consolidated audit and recovered-result JSON files. Each comparison records the dataset, reference source, and unit of analysis.  5.1   Data groups, evaluation measures, and uncertainty  For principle classification, Top-1 agreement is the share of passages whose highest-ranked principle matches the recorded label. Top-2 agreement is the share whose recorded label appears among the two highest-ranked principles. Top-2 gives an analyst a short candidate list. A higher Top-2 value does not mean better accuracy when only one answer is allowed. Precision shows how reliable a predicted category is. If 100 passages receive an environmental- principle prediction and 90 carry that reference label, precision is 90%. Recall shows how much of a reference category is found. If 100 passages carry the environmental label and the classifier finds 80, recall is 80%. F1 balances precision and recall through the harmonic mean:  F   1 k   =   2 P k R k  P k   +   R k  ,   MacroF1 =  1 9  9 ∑︂  k =1  F   1 k .   (8) Macro-F1 gives each principle equal weight, so the largest class cannot determine the entire score. Support means the number of reference examples for a principle. The references are weak labels. A result described as correct therefore means agreement with the recorded assignment, not an independent judgement of the passage’s meaning. A 95% confidence interval shows uncertainty in an estimate under the stated sampling method. For classification and mapping, the audit uses 2,000 bootstrap samples with seed 4206. Companies are sampled with replacement, and all passages from a selected CIN are kept together. This CIN-cluster method accounts for passages from the same company being related. Paired comparisons use the same sampled companies for both methods. These intervals describe variation within the available data; label errors and earlier exposure during model development remain outside that estimate. The 20-company score comparison uses 10,000 bootstrap samples of company-score pairs with seed 42. No detector intervals were calculated.  5.2   Method comparisons and generalisation checks  Table 2 summarises three comparisons: results by label source, performance on concepts excluded from training, and supervised versus zero-shot mapping.   The table records the examples and training conditions for each comparison. These are method and data-split comparisons rather than a controlled change to one component. The reported comparisons use the final labelled split and the training conditions listed in the table. Domain adaptation is part of the final model’s training sequence. 7   Discussion and Practical Use  7.1   How the outputs work together  GRASP connects three levels of analysis.   Passage-level outputs identify likely principles and language flags. Filing-level outputs organise reported figures and calculate the four score components. Company and sector views then place those outputs within a broader reporting context.   This structure lets an analyst move from a summary score to the underlying passage or filed item. The classifier, language detector, and Transparency Score serve different purposes. The classifier ranks regulatory principles against filing-derived labels. The language detector selects passages for wording review. The score combines reported-item coverage, evidence markers, language flags, and mapped SDG breadth. The evaluation in Section 5 reports the data group and reference source for each output.  7.2   Reading the evaluation results  Source-wise results show how the classifier responds to explicitly tagged passages, concept-mapped passages, and principle notes. Tests on excluded concepts add a second view by changing which reporting questions appear in labelled training.   Together, these comparisons describe model behaviour beyond the overall agreement value. The company-separated split defines the labelled training and test groups. The checkpoint checks establish which saved parameters produced the reported results.   Bootstrap intervals describe variation under company resampling, and paired comparisons evaluate both methods on the same selected companies. These recorded conditions make the comparisons clear and repeatable [11]. The principle-mapping result reuses the classifier evaluation, while the API check records successful model loading for one company.  7.3   Reading company and sector scores  The component breakdown explains how each company reaches the combined score. Completeness describes accepted responses across the fixed concept list.   Specificity records evidence-marker presence. Clarity records passages without a vagueness flag, and SDG breadth counts goals linked through the configured principle map. Showing all four components lets an analyst identify the part of the disclosure that drives a score difference. Sector comparisons use the saved industry groups and latest available filings. Year-wise comparisons use the eight companies with paired reports. These views describe the available company records under the same scoring rules. Detailed filing context, component values, and year labels support direct inspection of each comparison.  7.4   Use by analysts  An analyst can begin with a company or sector summary, select a component, inspect the source passage, and check the reported measure, period, and unit. Every flag retains the rule and source behind the decision.   The service therefore supports a complete path from review priority to supporting material. The four reporting levels also support different review tasks. A worked company example explains the calculation. Comparisons within a sector reveal different component patterns. The full financial group shows the score distribution, and the all-sector summary supports wider comparison. The numerical and assurance branches supply records for context review, while the reported evaluation identifies the specific component measured by each metric. 23

8   Conclusion  Large sustainability-report collections require a clear path from narrative claims to filed evidence and company-level summaries.   GRASP provides this path through structured BRSR storage, filing-derived labels, principle classification, language checks, numerical review, and a four-part Transparency Score. Passages and figures remain linked to the same filing. Label sources remain visible during evaluation, and every score component has an explicit calculation. The resulting workflow combines passage review, company scoring, and sector comparison in one service. The recovered classifier agrees with weak labels on 93.00% of test passages (95% CI: 92.04–93.89%) and reaches macro-F1 of 0.9158. The test set contains 6,201 passages from 175 companies excluded from supervised training. Agreement is 63.35% for explicitly tagged narratives, 95.15% for concept- mapped narratives, and 90.72% for principle notes. The fixed text-vagueness detector reaches F1 of 0.7436 on 80 development examples. The Transparency Score has Pearson correlation   r   = 0 . 6314 with 20 historical human ratings (95% CI: 0.2683–0.8519).   These findings describe principle assignment, language screening, and score comparison under the evaluation conditions in Section 5. The saved outputs cover 1,164 companies across 72 recorded sectors. Results move through four levels: one worked company, selected companies within a sector, the complete financial-sector group, and all sectors. Financial-company scores range from 29.83 to 67.56. Among the 47 sectors containing at least five companies, Wearing Apparel has the lowest mean, 42.33, and Warehousing and Transport Support has the highest, 54.55. Across the eight companies with paired-year scores, the mean rises by 5.23 points, from 45.17 to 50.40. Six scores rise and two fall. Component changes explain these movements within the available group. Company, sector, and year views make the saved results easy to inspect from both detailed and summary perspectives. This work can be extended using multiple levels. At the data level, collection can include annexures, charts, and additional annual filings. At the modelling level, expanded principle-labelled datasets and blind human-rating studies can support new model comparisons. Adaptation using declared training-company text can be evaluated on newly collected company groups. Business descriptions can support more detailed sector assignment and indicator-applicability rules. At the numerical- review level, extensions can compare measure definitions, units, periods, and business boundaries before generating review records. At the longitudinal level, additional annual reports can support repeated comparisons of the same companies under a recorded score version. At the framework level, the filing-based approach can be studied for international sustainability standards through explicit reporting-item mappings and separate evaluation in each setting.
